extracted.intended_audience: IP office staff, patent attorneys, policymakers, and researchers using IP statistics
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes legal standards, procedural requirements and data-collection rules across IP systems (patents, utility models, trademarks, designs, geographical indications) including patentability criteria, PCT and treaty procedures, and WIPO statistical methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is granted to an invention that meets the standards of novelty, non-obviousness and industrial applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents are valid for a limited period (generally 20 years). In return for time-limited exclusive rights, applicants are obliged to disclose their inventions to the public so that they may be replicated by others skilled in the art. The decision to grant a patent remains the prerogative of national or regional patent offices, which apply national law.

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT procedure stages and national-phase rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The PCT application process begins with the international phase (international search and optional preliminary examination and supplementary international search) and concludes with the national phase, during which national or regional patent offices decide on patentability according to national law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PCT simplifies multiple filings by delaying separate national filings, but actual grant decisions are made by each national/regional office in the national phase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model system characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility models confer rights similar to patents but differ in terms and examination: UMs are issued for a shorter period (6–10 years) and at most offices protection is granted without substantive examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term and procedures vary by office; in some jurisdictions 'utility model' covers protections similar to short-term patents (e.g., Republic of Ireland). Rights are limited to the jurisdiction of the issuing authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure and deposit requirement for microorganisms (Budapest Treaty)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an invention involves microorganisms, national laws in most countries require the applicant to deposit a sample at a designated International Depositary Authority (IDA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the Budapest Treaty, a deposit with any IDA is sufficient for patent procedures in all contracting states. An IDA is a scientific institution (typically a culture collection) capable of storing microorganisms. (As of September 2025 there were 52 IDAs.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark fundamentals and maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: A trademark is a sign used to distinguish the goods or services of one enterprise from those of another; the holder of a registered trademark has the exclusive right to use the mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trademark registrations can be maintained indefinitely provided renewal fees are paid. Procedures are governed by national/regional laws and rights are limited to the jurisdiction of registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Madrid System procedures and benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Madrid System allows filing a single international trademark application in one of the system languages (English, French, Spanish), paying a single set of fees, and indicating designated Madrid members where protection is sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Madrid System simplifies management (central recording of changes and renewals). A registration in the International Register has the same effect as a registration in each designated Contracting Party unless the national authority issues a refusal within a specified time period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design protection standards and term
rubrics_metrics.description: Designs protect the ornamental or aesthetic aspects of a useful article and can be protected if they are new or original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design rights are limited to the issuing jurisdiction. Registrations may be obtained nationally or via the Hague System. The term is generally five years and may be renewed in additional five-year periods up to a total of around 15 years in most cases. In some countries, designs are protected via design patents rather than registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical indications (GI) definitional standard and protection routes
rubrics_metrics.description: A geographical indication is a sign identifying a good as having originated in a specific geographical area and possessing a given quality, reputation or other characteristic essentially attributable to its geographical origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GIs can be protected through various legal means (sui generis systems, trademark law, regional systems, international agreements and other national legal means). The core function is to signal a link between product qualities and place of origin; national-level protection is often shared among several agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: GI data collection categories (WIPO GI questionnaire)
rubrics_metrics.description: WIPO's GI questionnaire collects data on GIs in force broken down by legal means of protection (sui generis, trademarks, international agreements), by origin (national/foreign) and by product types (agricultural products, wines and spirits, handicrafts, services, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GI data collected via the annual survey inform WIPO statistics; respondents may have difficulty identifying GIs protected through trademark systems, and reporting practices vary by jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: WIPO annual IP statistics surveys and questionnaire coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: WIPO collects IP data from national and regional IP offices through annual surveys consisting of 27 questionnaires, available in Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian and Spanish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data are entered into the WIPO Statistics Database; continuous efforts are made to improve quality and availability and to gather data from as many IP offices as possible. The long-established survey covers patents, utility models, trademarks, designs and plant varieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimating world totals and handling missing data
rubrics_metrics.description: World totals for applications and grants/registrations are WIPO estimates because data are not available for every IP office each year; missing data are estimated using methods such as linear extrapolation and averaging adjacent data points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an office provides data not broken down by origin, WIPO estimates resident and non-resident counts using historical shares recorded at that office. The estimation method depends on the year and office; most large offices provide data, so only small shares are estimated.

rubrics_metrics.name: International comparability caveats for IP statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: IP statistics are compiled based on harmonized definitions to facilitate international comparison, but national laws, filing practices and statistical reporting may vary between jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of continual updating and revision of historical statistics, figures in this report may differ from previous editions and from data on WIPO's website; users should interpret comparisons with caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: World Bank income classification thresholds used in analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Economies are classified using 2024 gross national income per capita (World Bank Atlas method) into: low-income (USD 1,135 or less), lower middle-income (USD 1,136 to USD 4,495), upper middle-income (USD 4,496 to USD 13,935) and high-income (over USD 13,935).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These classifications are used in the report's breakdowns and regional analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling double counting for regional systems (GI counting rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: To minimize double counting, GIs in force through regional systems (e.g., EU) and the Lisbon System were counted once only rather than multiplied by the number of member states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite this, the overall total may still include a degree of double counting because GIs protected through bilateral, plurilateral or multilateral agreements could potentially be included multiple times; the report flags this limitation and advises caution in interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for breaks in national data series (CNIPA 2017 example)
rubrics_metrics.description: A change in the method used by CNIPA in 2017 for counting applications (from including all applications received to including only those for which fees were paid) created a break in the series for China for 2017 and 2018 that makes comparisons with previous years not meaningful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because China accounts for a large share of global applications, this break affects worldwide growth comparisons for those years; the report excludes 2017 growth for certain figures and flags the inconsistency.
